frameworks.name: One Big Idea + Ten Reasons
frameworks.definition: Marketing message structure: consolidate multiple product benefits into a single overarching value proposition supported by ten distinct supporting reasons, rather than ten separate claims each with one supporting reason.

claims.text: Clarity beats cleverness in all messaging contexts: copy, sales pitches, emails, and content creation. The longer Alex Hormozi has been in business, the more he emphasizes clarity over cleverness and simplicity over complexity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Audience reach is a funnel of successive exclusion: of 100 people who register for an offer, fewer than 50% will show up; of 1,000 people who see an ad, fewer than 2% will click. This small conversion percentage means trying to be clever in messaging is strategically incorrect.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: With conversion rates this low, message clarity is the binding constraint, not novelty or creativity.
bounded_by: Does not specify the product category or audience type these percentages apply to

claims.text: Message compression and simplification—iteratively shortening and clarifying a message until it becomes elegant—is where effectiveness emerges. The effort of continuous compression yields elegance and impact.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: The campaign structure 'One Big Benefit + Ten Reasons' outperforms the structure 'Ten Big Ideas + One Reason Each' in conversion rate. A marketer who consolidated his company's 10-product offerings into a single unified value prop with 10 supporting reasons achieved his highest-converting campaign in company history after implementing this shift.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Consolidation reduces cognitive load on the buyer and anchors all supporting reasons to a single decision frame, eliminating the mental friction of parallel options.
bounded_by: Example was a high-performing marketer in an established large company; applicability to early-stage or single-product businesses unclear

claims.text: Repetition of the same core message across many iterations is the core scaling mechanism for campaigns. Alex Hormozi created approximately 5,000 ads that all communicated the same essential message for a book launch, yet the vast majority of his audience still did not learn about it, register, or attend.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Large existing audience (sufficient scale that 5,000 similar ads can be created and distributed)
claims.mechanism: Repetition across high volume of distributed messages ensures that sufficient percentage of the large target audience encounters the message. Low click-through rates require volume multiplication to reach absolute numbers.
bounded_by: Even with 5,000 repetitions of the same message, most of the audience still did not find out, register, or attend. The mechanism works only on percentages, not absolute persuasion of everyone.

examples.text: A phenomenal marketer at a successful large company had built a complex marketing structure with 10 separate things to sell. After spending a day with Alex Hormozi and receiving feedback to consolidate into one big benefit supported by 10 reasons, the marketer restructured the entire campaign and achieved the highest conversion rate in the company's history. The marketer later told Hormozi: 'My team has heard me say this so many times. They needed somebody from the outside to say it.' This illustrates the power of outside validation for internal changes teams already intellectually understand.

For a book launch, Alex Hormozi created approximately 5,000 ads that all essentially said the same thing. Despite this massive repetition, the majority of his audience never learned about the launch, the majority of those who did learn didn't register, and the majority of those who registered didn't attend. The launch still broke records and achieved all sales and donation goals. This illustrates that even with extreme message repetition and successful outcomes, the audience-funnel percentages remain brutally low, requiring volume thinking rather than persuasion thinking.

practices.text: When writing copy, crafting sales pitches, writing emails, or creating content, use the structure: one big idea with ten reasons supporting it, rather than ten big ideas each with one reason.

Continuously compress and simplify your message; iterate until the message becomes as clear and simple as humanly possible. The repeated effort of compression is where elegance and effectiveness emerge.
Create high volume of variations on your core message rather than trying to craft single clever pieces. Repeat the same essential message across thousands of distribution instances.
